title: Self-Adaptive Perturbation Radii for Adversarial Training

problem.claim: Adversarial training can substantially degrade performance on clean data while protecting models from adversarial samples.

gap.claim: Searching for an adaptive perturbation radius for each training sample creates a conflict between exact searching and computational overhead.

contributions.claim: The paper shows the superiority of adaptive perturbation radii for accuracy and robustness.
The paper proposes a self-adaptive adjustment framework for perturbation radii that avoids tedious searching.
The framework is discussed for deep neural networks and kernel support vector machines.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the self-adaptive perturbation-radius adjustment framework as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments show improved adversarial robustness without compromising natural generalization.
The authors report that the framework is competitive with existing searching strategies in running time.

narrative_sequence.summary: Adversarial training is presented as an effective defense against imperceptible adversarial samples.
Adversarial training can significantly reduce clean-data performance.
Adaptive perturbation radii may improve clean and adversarial performance, but exact per-sample searching incurs computational overhead.
The paper presents a self-adaptive perturbation-radius adjustment framework and discusses it for DNNs and kernel SVMs.
The authors report improved robustness without compromising natural generalization and competitive running time.

source_observation.claim: Per-sample adaptive perturbation radii are presented as a way to balance clean-data accuracy and adversarial robustness.

interpretation.claim: Training robustness need not rely on one fixed perturbation scale for all samples.

application.claim: When robustness and natural performance conflict, consider sample-specific perturbation control with an efficient adjustment mechanism.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify when adaptive radii fail or how their computational cost scales.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide the framework's adjustment rule or optimization details.
The abstract does not report datasets, baselines, quantitative results, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported findings.
